name: Joab
bio:
Joab was the son of Zeruiah, brother of Abishai and Asahel, and David's most important military commander — fierce, ruthless, and loyal to David's dynasty, yet repeatedly acting on his own authority and without scruple.

When Abner installed Ish-Bosheth as king and war broke out with the house of David, Joab's forces clashed with Abner's at the pool of Gibeon, beginning with a contest between young men and escalating into full battle, which Joab's side won. Joab's brother Asahel, swift as a wild gazelle, chased Abner relentlessly; Abner warned him off several times, reluctant to kill him, but Asahel would not turn aside, so Abner struck him dead with the butt of his spear (2 Samuel 2:12-23).

When Abner later defected to David and came to Hebron to negotiate peace, David welcomed him and sent him away safely; but Joab, on learning of it, angrily confronted David for letting Abner go, then secretly sent messengers to bring him back, pulled him aside at the city gate under pretense of private conversation, and stabbed him to death in revenge for Asahel (2 Samuel 3:22-27). David was furious and publicly cursed Joab's house, yet could do nothing against Zeruiah's two sons, saying, "Today... I am weak, though anointed king, and these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too strong for me" (2 Samuel 3:28-39).

When David, newly anointed king over all Israel, marched on Jerusalem to take it from its Jebusite inhabitants, David declared that whoever struck the Jebusites first would become chief and captain; Joab was the one who went up first, winning him that place of command, and he went on to rebuild the rest of the city while David fortified the citadel (1 Chronicles 11:4-8).

Once David's kingdom was secure, Joab was placed over the army as part of David's royal administration, a position of immense power he would hold for most of the rest of David's reign (2 Samuel 8:16).

When the Ammonites under Hanun hired Aramean mercenaries against Israel, Joab led the army out, splitting his forces between himself, facing the Arameans, and his brother Abishai, facing the Ammonites, with the agreement that each would help the other if hard pressed; both sides routed their enemies (2 Samuel 10:7-14). The next year, Joab led the siege of the Ammonite capital, Rabbah; it was during this campaign that David, remaining behind in Jerusalem, sent for Bathsheba and later ordered Joab, through a letter carried by Uriah himself, to place Uriah in the fiercest fighting and withdraw so he would be killed — an order Joab carried out without recorded objection, then carefully coached his messenger on how to break the news of the resulting casualties to David (2 Samuel 11:1, 6-25). Joab finally captured Rabbah's water supply and, rather than take the final glory for himself, sent word for David to come lead the last assault and claim the city in his own name; David did so, taking the Ammonite king's gold crown for his own head (2 Samuel 12:26-31). Noticing that David's heart had turned toward the exiled Absalom, Joab arranged for a wise woman of Tekoa to tell the king a crafted parable that maneuvered him into permitting Absalom's return; Joab then personally went to Geshur and brought Absalom back to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 14:1-23). When Absalom, frustrated at still being refused an audience with David, set Joab's barley field on fire to force his attention, Joab finally went to him and arranged the reconciliation Absalom wanted (2 Samuel 14:29-33). When the decisive battle against Absalom's rebellion came, David divided his army into three, with Joab commanding one division alongside Abishai and Ittai the Gittite, and ordered all three, within earshot of the whole army, to deal gently with Absalom for his sake. The battle, fought in the forest of Ephraim, became a rout, with the forest itself claiming more lives than the sword; Absalom himself, fleeing on a mule, was caught by his famously heavy hair in the branches of a great oak and left hanging helplessly between heaven and earth (2 Samuel 18:1-9). When a soldier reported this to Joab rather than killing Absalom on the spot, citing the king's order, Joab refused to waste the moment: he took three javelins and plunged them into Absalom's heart while he still hung alive in the tree, and ten of Joab's armor-bearers finished the killing, directly defying David's explicit command (2 Samuel 18:10-15). Joab had the army stand down, had Absalom's body thrown into a pit in the forest and covered with a great heap of stones, and later refused to let Ahimaaz carry news of the victory to David, since it meant reporting the king's son's death; he sent a man named Cushi instead (2 Samuel 18:16-21). When David shut himself away weeping for Absalom instead of greeting his victorious army, Joab confronted him bluntly, warning that he had humiliated the men who had just saved his life and the lives of his whole family, and that unless he went out at once to encourage them, David would lose every last follower by nightfall; David heeded him and went out to sit in the gate (2 Samuel 19:1-8). After Judah invited David home, David offered Joab's command to his cousin Amasa, who had led Absalom's army, apparently as punishment for killing Absalom against orders (2 Samuel 19:13).

When Sheba son of Bichri led Israel into a fresh revolt, David sent Amasa to muster Judah's forces, but when Amasa took longer than the time David had set, David sent Abishai and Joab's men after Sheba instead. At the great stone in Gibeon, Joab met Amasa on the road; with his sword concealed and apparently falling loose, Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand as if to kiss him in greeting, then drove the hidden sword into his belly with his left, spilling his insides to the ground and killing him instantly — reclaiming command of the army by murdering the cousin David had appointed over him, just as he had once murdered Abner (2 Samuel 20:1-13). Joab then pursued Sheba to the city of Abel Beth Maacah and besieged it, until a wise woman of the city negotiated with him, and the residents threw Sheba's severed head over the wall to end the siege (2 Samuel 20:14-22). When the LORD's anger moved David to order a census of Israel and Judah, Joab objected, asking the king why he wanted to do such a thing, but David's command prevailed; Joab and the army commanders spent over nine months traveling the whole land to count the fighting men before returning with the total (2 Samuel 24:1-9). As David grew old, Joab backed Adonijah's attempt to seize the throne, alongside the priest Abiathar — but Solomon was crowned instead, and Adonijah's bid collapsed (1 Kings 1:7-10, 41). On his deathbed, David specifically charged Solomon not to let Joab's grey head go to the grave in peace, recalling the blood of Abner and Amasa that Joab had shed in peacetime and worn like a badge (1 Kings 2:5-6). When Solomon later moved to execute Adonijah for a renewed claim to the throne, Joab, realizing his own danger, fled to the tabernacle and grasped the horns of the altar for sanctuary; Solomon sent Benaiah to strike him down there anyway, ending the life of David's most formidable and most ruthless commander (1 Kings 2:28-34).
